paragraphs: §1 — The Muslims took over the Christian consensus on Jesus' miracles without scrutiny

As for the companions of Jesus and those who are ascribed to him — namely the Christians (al-naṣārā) — they claimed divinity (al-rubūbiyya) for him, according to what we have related of their doctrine. As for the founder of the Muslims (ṣāḥib al-Muslimīn), when he laid claim to prophethood (al-nubuwwa) he looked to the consensus of the Christians upon the miracles (muʿjizāt) of Jesus; and he was no investigator (baḥḥāth) and no examiner (naẓẓār), such as would look into the root of the report. So he conceded to him [Jesus] the miracles, lest what he himself was aiming at be undone for him, and because he was loth — [knowing] that if he gave the lie to that, it would not be safe that he himself, in turn, would [also] be given the lie to after him, after the manner of what we have mentioned concerning the affair of Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī. So he did not assent to the Christians in conceding the divinity (lāhūt) of Jesus — but rather they [the Muslims] invalidated the divinity — while he did assent to the Christians and agreed with them that he was born of no father.

: The preamble frames the whole bab as an exposure of a borrowed premise. The Muslim kalām case for Jesus' prophethood, Q argues, rests not on independent verification but on the Christian consensus about Jesus' miracles — a consensus Muhammad (the unnamed ṣāḥib al-Muslimīn, Q's standing periphrasis) accepted uncritically (he was "no baḥḥāth and no naẓẓār"), and accepted selectively: he kept the miracles but rejected the divinity, just as he feared his own claim might be undermined if he undercut a fellow claimant — the logic Q ties to the case of Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (the 8th-c. messianic claimant of M1's sect-catalogue), which §7 will close on. The muʿjiza (evidentiary miracle, iʿjāz) / nubuwwa terminology is the prophetological apparatus staged in glossary §VII; Q deploys it here turned against the Muslim and Christian claims at once.
§2 — The argument from mass-transmission, and its self-defeating parallel in the transmission of the divinity

Among that which the Muslim mutakallimūn adduce as an argument for the prophethood of Jesus is their saying: We have observed the Christians, who are a numerous multitude and a community whose number cannot be reckoned, upon the like of whom collusion (al-tawāṭuʾ) is not admissible; and they have reported that they transmitted from their forefathers that Jesus son of Mary came with miracles — the reviving of the dead, the opening of the eye of the blind, and other of his deeds, the like of which it is not admissible should come save from the Lord of the worlds, and which come about only at the hand of a messenger (rasūl). Since that is so, it is established that Jesus is a prophet, a messenger from God.

They said: now if an opponent should rebut us by alleging that those who transmitted the proof-signs (aʿlām) of Jesus are, all of them, the very ones who [also] transmitted his divinity, and that he is one of the three hypostases (al-aqānīm al-thalātha) which are God (great and exalted be He), and that God was united (ittaḥada) with his body — so that, if they are truthful in their transmission of his miracles, then they are likewise truthful in their transmission of his divinity — we say to him: the rebuttal is null, and what you have said and rebutted with is not on a par with the ground we relied upon and in which we exhibited transmission (al-naql). For their transmission of the miracles was [transmission] from those who witnessed them and reported them; whereas the matter of the divinity is only something they claimed by way of the intelligible (min jihat al-maʿqūl) — and its corruption is plain and manifest. And that in which the intelligible, analogy (al-qiyās), and the establishing of demonstration (al-burhān) by way of speculation (al-naẓar) are claimed, its course is not the course of what is established by report (al-khabar) and eyewitness (al-mushāhada). For when we say to the Christians, "what is the proof that Jesus came with signs and miracles?" they say, "because we transmitted that from our forefathers, age after age — that those who were in his age witnessed him doing that in their presence." But if we say, "what is the proof that he is an attribute of the attributes of God (great and exalted be He)?" they mention neither transmission nor eyewitness, but rather adduce that by way of analogy and the intelligible.

: Q sets out the Muslim mutakallimūn's tawātur argument (mass-transmission by a multitude incapable of collusion, tawāṭuʾ, establishes the miracles as fact) and the natural Christian rejoinder (the same transmitters also transmit the divinity, so accept both or neither). The Muslim reply Q reports is methodologically sharp: miracles are matters of report and eyewitness (khabar wa-mushāhada), transmissible by naql; the divinity is a matter claimed only min jihat al-maʿqūl — by reasoning, qiyās, and naẓar — and so is not underwritten by the transmission at all. The epistemological distinction (transmitted fact vs. inferred doctrine) is genuine Bahshamī uṣūl (see glossary §III on naql, naẓar, burhān, qiyās) — and Q will now show, in §3, that the Muslims have misstated the rebuttal and that it cannot be parried this way.
§3 — The transmitters of Jesus' miracles also transmit Paul's; if Paul is a prophet, the Trinity is true — so the whole transmission collapses

It is said to them: you have distorted the rebuttal and diverted it from its meaning, and this that you have said is not that with which you are being rebutted. Rather, what is said to you is: those who transmitted the miracles of Jesus — namely the Christians — are, all of them, the very ones who claimed prophethood for the four disciples, who are Matthew, Luke, Mark, and John, and reported of them that they performed signs and wonders. And of the same kind, they claimed for Paul (Būluṣ) that he was a prophet, and that Jesus gave him tidings and sent him and gave him signs and miracles, and that it was he who brought most of mankind into the religion of Christianity — such as the Romans (al-Rūm) and others; and that those who witnessed his miracles were more than those who witnessed the miracles of Jesus — since Jesus was only in the land of Syria (arḍ al-Shaʾm) alone, whereas Paul entered the land of the Romans and went round through many lands calling people, and used to perform the miracles in every place he entered. By that, people submitted to him and entered into what he called them to; so the transmitters from him are more numerous than the transmitters of the report of Jesus.

And it was Paul who was the most open in the statement of the Trinity (al-tathlīth) and declared explicitly that the Creator (mighty and exalted) is a substance [in] three hypostases (jawhar thalāthat aqānīm) — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — and that Jesus is the Son of God and His knowledge (ʿilmuhu), and that he is one of the hypostases. So if the transmission of the Christians of the miracles of Jesus is a sound transmission, and they were truthful in that, then likewise their transmission of the miracles of Paul must be [a case in which] they are truthful — nay, the miracles of Paul must be the better-attested, since those who transmitted them — by what we have been informed — are several times those who transmitted the miracles of Jesus. And since that is so, and the prophethood of Paul had been established [thereby], then everything he said is true; so his statement of the Trinity, and that the Creator is a substance [in] three hypostases, would be a sound statement.

Now if they say: and how can the statement of the Trinity be a sound statement, when the intellects (al-ʿuqūl) corrupt it and render it impossible? — we say: if that is so, then it is [thereby] nullified that the one who reported that was a prophet or came with a miracle, and it is established for us that those who transmitted that from them were not a people by whom the proof is established (tathbutu bihim al-ḥujja), and that those who allege that "a numerous multitude, by whose statement the proof is established, witnessed that" are liars in their claim. And once the mendacity of those who claimed the miracles for Paul is established, and those who reported the miracles of Jesus were [fewer] than they — and some of them [in any case] were the more deserving to be charged with the lie — then the statement of whoever claims the prophethood of Jesus is nullified. And once the prophethood of Jesus is nullified — and [the prophethood] of others whom Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī invested with prophethood — then what he himself claimed of prophethood is [likewise] nullified.

: The hinge of the bab. Q's complaint (§3 opening) is that the Muslims re-described the rebuttal: the live objection is not "they transmit the divinity too" (a doctrine) but "they transmit, on identical tawātur grounds, the miracles of Paul and of the four evangelists" (matters of khabar wa-mushāhada, exactly the category the Muslims privileged). Q then springs the dilemma: Paul's miracles are by the Muslims' own criterion better attested than Jesus' (more transmitters, wider geography — Paul evangelized the Romans across "many lands," Jesus only arḍ al-Shaʾm); so Paul's prophethood is established; so Paul's explicit Trinitarianism (jawhar thalāthat aqānīm — Father/Son/Holy-Spirit) is true. But the Trinity "the intellects corrupt and render impossible" (the rational refutation of Babs 1–4). Therefore the transmission-chain proves a falsehood, which voids it as a ḥujja — and with it the prophethood of Jesus, and, by the §1 linkage, the prophethood-claims of Abū ʿĪsā. This is a clean reductio: the transmitters who certify Jesus certify Paul, who certifies the (rationally impossible) Trinity, so the whole transmission fails to "establish the proof." On al-Rūm = the (Christian, uncircumcised) Byzantines, cf. Bab 14 §§14–15.
§4 — If the Muslims fall back on Muhammad's testimony, they impale themselves on the Jewish transmission of the Torah's perpetuity

So if the Muslims abandon the argument for the prophethood of Jesus from the standpoint of the report of the Christians, and fall back on [the claim] that this was established for them only by the statement of their own founder (ṣāḥibihim), whose prophethood has [in their view] been established — and likewise the moderns (al-muḥdathūn) among the Muslim mutakallimūn have come to say, regarding Moses also, that they establish his prophethood only from the report of their own founder, but as for what the Jews and the Christians transmit, then no (and this is contrary to what the ancients (al-qudamāʾ) of their mutakallimūn used to hold and say, such as Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf and Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām and others) — [then we reply as follows].

What drove these moderns to this statement was two things. The one: what distressed them in the disputation of the Jews and the latter's binding them [with the argument] that, if they conceded that the report of the Jews necessitates knowledge and that the proof is established by it, then it must follow that what they [the Jews] transmitted of the perpetuity of the Law (taʾbīd al-sharīʿa) is a sound transmission — and by that the report of their own founder is nullified. And the second: that their founder alleged that the report of him is found in the Torah, and that Moses gave good tidings of him and of his coming-forth (mabʿathihi); whereas we, all of us, say that this is false, since when we investigated we did not find that in the Torah. So the matter compelled them [the Muslims] to deny what he [their founder] had affirmed of the Torah and adduced as testimony from it and from its people, in more than one place of his book — [all] of which we have set out exhaustively in the book we composed against them.

: The Muslims' first retreat: drop the borrowed Christian transmission and rest Jesus' (and Moses') prophethood on Muhammad's own testimony alone. Q notes this is a modern position (the muḥdathūn) at odds with the qudamāʾ — naming Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf (d. c. 227/841) and his nephew Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām (d. c. 231/845), the great early Basran Muʿtazila, who did credit Jewish/Christian tawātur. Q diagnoses two pressures behind the shift: (a) the Jewish ilzām — if Jewish mass-transmission yields knowledge, then the Jews' transmitted taʾbīd al-sharīʿa (perpetuity/non-abrogation of the Law) is certain, which destroys Islam's abrogation-claim; (b) the embarrassment that the Qurʾānic claim that the Torah foretells Muhammad (his mabʿath) fails on inspection — "we did not find that in the Torah." Q cross-refers to his lost dedicated anti-Muslim work ("the book we composed against them"). Taʾbīd al-sharīʿa is the same anti-abrogation (naskh) thesis argued scripturally in Bab 6 §§8–12.
§5 — Their second move: "your Torah and your Moses are not the true ones" — which contradicts their own founder

So they alleged that this Torah which is in your hands is not the true, original Torah, and that the Moses by whom you [Jews] swear is not the one by whom we swear. So when we said to them, "and why have you alleged that?" they made what is binding upon them, and that by which we impugn them, into the answer. They said: because Moses the true prophet is the one who gave good tidings of Muhammad, and the true Torah is the one in which that is recorded; so when you yourselves alleged that this Torah which is in your hands does not have that recorded in it, and that the Moses by whom you swear did not [...] inform of that, we knew that this Moses and this Torah are other than those [first ones].

: The second retreat, and a circular one. Pressed on why the Jewish Torah cannot be the standard, the Muslims convert the very point in dispute (does the Torah foretell Muhammad?) into the premise of an answer: the true Torah/Moses by definition foretell Muhammad; the extant Torah/Moses do not; therefore the extant ones are spurious. Q's note (carried into §6) is that this both (a) begs the question and (b) flatly contradicts their own founder, who had repeatedly invoked this Torah and its adherents as witnesses. The em-dashed "[...] inform" marks a syntactic seam at the p194→p193 page-fold ("لم ... نُخْبِرُ"); the sense is secure ("did not inform of that"), only the surface phrasing is rough in the OCR — no lacuna of content.
§6 — That position contradicts their founder, abolishes their own tawātur, and is refuted by the al-Maʾmūn-assembly analogy

So by this statement they are [shown to be] contradicting their own principles — as we have said — giving the lie to their own founder in his verification of this Torah and his adducing of its people as witnesses in many places. And moreover, along with that, they have [thereby] invalidated the argument from mass-transmission (ḥujjat al-tawātur) upon which they rely in establishing reports; and they have ascribed to the Creator (great and mighty be He) that He neglected creation from the cutting-off of prophethood until the coming of Muhammad, and left them with no proof, no command, and no prohibition. For if, before Muhammad, there was no report and no transmission of a prophet save the transmission of the Jews and the Christians, and that was something by which no proof is established, then the proof and the reports of the prophets are [all] nullified. And some of them, under this binding [argument], were driven to allege that people were [in that interval] held to worship by what was in their intellects (mā fī ʿuqūlihim) — and we have already shown the corruption of this statement in Bab 14 of this Maqala, and shown that it issues in the nullification of prophethood; and we have shown also, in the bab before this one, the corruption of the prophethood of their founder from another angle, in what contains an exposition for whoever ponders it.

Then it is said to them, concerning their inference that the Moses by whom you swear is not the true prophet Moses, by what we have related from them: Inform us about a people who were present in the assembly (majlis) of one of the caliphs — say, al-Maʾmūn or another — and he ordered, in their presence, some command; then they went out from before him and dispersed; then they met in some place, in some town, and one of them said to another: "Do you not know that we were, on such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month of such-and-such a year, at Baghdad, in the assembly of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAbd Allāh al-Maʾmūn son of Hārūn al-Rashīd, brother of Muhammad al-Amīn son of Zubayda, and that he ordered such-and-such?" — and others of them said: "We too were present on that day, as you have mentioned; but as for this which you allege he ordered, he did not order it; rather what he ordered was the contrary of this, namely such-and-such." Does it follow, from this statement, and from their disagreement, and from each party's claiming the contrary of what the other party claimed, that ʿAbd Allāh the Commander of the Faithful al-Maʾmūn son of Hārūn al-Rashīd, brother of Muhammad al-Amīn son of Zubayda, is other than the one against whom the other party claimed what it claimed? Or does it rather follow that one of the two parties must have lied and claimed against him that he said what he did not say? Now if they alleged that this [al-Maʾmūn] is other than that [al-Maʾmūn], then this is the utmost of impudent calumny (al-baht), and it would not be worth holding speech with them, since there was not known upon the earth anyone in whom these matters and these descriptions are combined other than him. And if they assent [to the alternative] — that this is that, and there is no escape from it, and that only one of the two parties added to him [a falsehood] and claimed that he said what he did not say — we say: just so do we likewise say that there was, in such-and-such an age, in the kingship of so-and-so, a man of the offspring of Jacob — who is Israel — and of the offspring of Levi, called Moses son of ʿImrān, and his brother Aaron, and his sister Miriam; and that God (great be His praise) addressed him from the bush of the bramble (shajarat al-ʿawsaj) and sent him to Pharaoh and to the Children of Israel with miraculous signs — namely the turning of the staff into a serpent, and the white hand, and the turning of the water into blood, and the cleaving of the sea, and the rest of what the Book has recorded of his miracles — and that He commanded him to command the Children of Israel to take up the Sabbath and the suspension of works on it, and the eating of unleavened bread (al-faṭīr) seven days, and circumcision, and other than that. And you yourselves assented to us in all these descriptions and these tokens, with no disagreement. Then we said that he took up the Law; and you alleged that he gave good tidings of so-and-so [Muhammad] and informed that he would come. Does it follow, from this statement, that the one of whom we informed is other than the one to whom you assented — or does it [not rather] follow that one of us must have added [a falsehood] to him, either we or you? And this is something there is no escape from. And in it is the demolition of this contrived, newly-fabricated opinion, and it is established that the Moses by whom we swear is the one to whom they themselves assented, and that the lie and the addition occurred only from one of the two parties. And it is not admissible that it should be we who lied and added, since we were scattered, dispersed from the east to the west: it is not admissible that we should all have colluded (natawāṭaʾ) upon denying what is recorded in our keeping. So if they say, "then likewise we too — scattered, dispersed from the east to the west — it is not admissible that we should lie," we say: you have not lied in the relating about the one who said that; rather you relate it [only] from a single one who said it and informed you of it — and the one who said it is the one who added [the falsehood] in that, in order to give by it the impression of the soundness of his affair. And if they fall back upon distortion (al-taḥrīf) and [forced] interpretation (al-taʾwīl), then what has passed concerning that has [already] passed, [and there is] no need for more.

: §6 is the bab's longest argument and its rhetorical climax — a triple charge plus a sustained analogy. The triple charge: the "spurious-Torah" move (a) contradicts the Muslims' own founder (who invoked this Torah), (b) abolishes the ḥujjat al-tawātur they need everywhere else, and (c) saddles God with abandoning humanity (no prophet, command, or prohibition) from the cessation of prophecy until Muhammad — the very predicament that drives some Muslims to the "people were bound by their ʿuqūl" claim Q refuted in Bab 14 (the "command-by-reason-alone" position that "issues in the nullification of prophethood"). The al-Maʾmūn-assembly analogy is the engine: two parties who disagree about what al-Maʾmūn ordered cannot thereby conclude there were two al-Maʾmūns; one party simply lied about the content. Transposed: Jews and Muslims agree on the entire identifying description of Moses (Levite, brother Aaron, sister Miriam, the burning ʿawsaj-bush, the staff/hand/blood/sea-cleaving signs, the Sabbath/maṣṣot/circumcision legislation) — so they speak of one Moses; they disagree only on the added claim "he foretold Muhammad," which is therefore the falsehood added by one party. And it cannot be the Jews who added it: a globally scattered nation cannot have colluded (tawāṭuʾ) to suppress something in their own canonical keeping, whereas the Muslim datum descends from a single originator (their founder) with motive to embellish. The choice of al-Maʾmūn (r. 198–218/813–833), with the precise genealogy (son of Hārūn al-Rashīd, brother of al-Amīn, son of Zubayda), dates Q's polemical milieu and is a nice touch of Baghdad local color. Baht (brazen calumny) and taḥrīf (distortion) are Q's standing anti-apologetic register (glossary §IX).
§7 — With Jesus' prophethood gone, the prophethood-claims built upon it — Abū ʿĪsā and Yūdghān — collapse

So now the statement of Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī is nullified, and his claim to prophethood — together with the prophethood of the two [Jesus and Muhammad] to whom he conceded that [prophethood]. As for the affair of Yūdghān, who is "the Shepherd" (al-Rāʿī), and his claim that he is the Messiah — there is no point in occupying oneself with it, since the matter in it is easier and slighter than to be mentioned. And now we turn to the refutation of whoever held the doctrine of transmigration (al-tanāsukh), from among the ʿĀnāniyya and others.

: The bab closes by collecting the bracketed payoff of §1's framing. Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī (the early-8th-c. Isfahani messianic-prophetic claimant whose sect, the ʿĪsāwiyya/Iṣfahāniyya, Q catalogues in M1) had — on Q's account — conceded the prophethood of both Jesus and Muhammad ("the two"); so once their prophethood is voided, the scaffolding under his claim falls with it. Yūdghān (Yūdghān al-Hamadhānī, al-Rāʿī "the Shepherd," founder of the Yūdghāniyya, a follower-current of Abū ʿĪsā) and his messianic claim Q dismisses as too feeble to bother refuting. The closing sentence is the explicit bridge to Bab 17, "On the refutation of whoever held the doctrine of transmigration (al-tanāsukh)," naming his next targets: the ʿĀnāniyya (the followers of ʿAnan b. David) "and others." On Q's treatment of these sects see Nemoy's "Account of the Jewish Sects," HUCA 7 (1930), the same study that anchors the published English control for the present bab.

- The bab's subject and structure. The heading is unambiguous: fī fasād qawl man iddaʿā li-ʿĪsā ibn Maryam al-nubuwwa wa-annahu qad atā bi-muʿjizāt — "on the corruption of the statement of whoever claimed for Jesus son of Mary prophethood, and that he came with miracles." But the bab's real target is broader than Jesus: it is an interlocking refutation of three prophethood-claims — Jesus', Muhammad's, and (closing the file's frame) Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī's — all of which Q shows to be load-bearing on a single, defective evidentiary structure. §1 frames the borrowing; §2 states the Muslim tawātur argument for Jesus' miracles and its Christian rejoinder; §3 detonates the reductio via Paul; §§4–6 chase the Muslim retreat (first to Muhammad's bare testimony, then to the "spurious-Torah" claim) and demolish it with the contradiction-of-the-founder charge and the al-Maʾmūn analogy; §7 collects the consequence for Abū ʿĪsā and Yūdghān and bridges to Bab 17.

- The Paul reductio (§3) is the conceptual core. Q's move is unusually elegant: he does not deny the Christian tawātur head-on but rides it to a contradiction. The same uncollusive multitude that certifies Jesus' miracles certifies Paul's — on the Muslims' own khabar/mushāhada criterion, more abundantly (Paul evangelized the Romans across many lands; Jesus was confined to Syria). So Paul's prophethood stands; so Paul's explicit Trinitarianism (jawhar thalāthat aqānīm) is true; but the Trinity is rationally impossible (the Bab 1–4 result). The transmission therefore certifies a known falsehood, which voids its probative force entirely. The argument cleverly weaponizes the Christians' high estimate of Paul against the Muslims' selective acceptance of Christian transmission.

- The al-Maʾmūn-assembly analogy (§6) is the most developed piece of reasoning in the bab and a small masterpiece of kalām dialectic. Its logical point: disagreement between two reliable mass-transmissions about what an agreed individual did never licenses positing two individuals; it licenses only the inference that one transmission contains an addition (a lie). Applied to Moses: Jews and Muslims share the entire identifying description (lineage, siblings, the ʿawsaj theophany, the five signs, the Sabbath/maṣṣot/circumcision legislation), so they denote one Moses; they differ only on the appended "foretold Muhammad," which is therefore the added falsehood — and provably not the Jews' addition, since a globe-scattered nation cannot collude to suppress its own canon, whereas the Muslim claim traces to a single interested originator. This is the tawāṭuʾ-impossibility argument (the backbone of Jewish anti-taḥrīf polemic) given a crisp dialectical form.

- Prophetology vocabulary (glossary §VII). This bab is the natural home for the staged prophetological anchor-terms: al-nubuwwa (prophethood), muʿjiza / muʿjizāt (evidentiary miracle[s]), al-iʿjāz (the miraculous/inimitable), rasūl (messenger), aʿlām (proof-signs). Rendered consistently with the Bab 5–6 Christological material; muʿjiza is kept as "miracle" with the technical evidentiary force flagged on first use, since the whole argument turns on the miracle as a probative sign of prophethood (the thing the transmission is supposed to certify).

- Polemical register. Q's anti-apologetic lexicon recurs: baht (brazen calumny/mendacity, §6), taḥrīf (distortion, §6), taʾwīl in its pejorative "forced interpretation" sense (§6) — all consistent with glossary §IX. Note the comparatively restrained register of this bab versus Bab 14's baht/qiḥḥa against the Christians: here the primary adversary is the Muslim mutakallim, handled with dialectical rather than abusive force.

- OCR / text state. The Arabic is clean and continuous across both files; the only rough seam is the p194→p193 page-fold in §5 (the "لم ... نُخْبِرُ" clause), where the surface syntax is slightly disordered but the sense ("did not inform of that") is secure — flagged in , no content lacuna. The diff-report records that Kraken's Hebrew runs on pp. 198/196/193 were garbage and the multimodal pass dropped them as "(missing)"; this is correct, because Bab 16 contains essentially no Hebrew biblical citations — the bracketed Kraken "Hebrew" was misread Arabic (the catalogue's dayyān im lo fragment at the very top belongs to the Bab 15 tail, which is excluded). The bab argues entirely from transmission-theory and analogy, not from prooftexts, so the absence of Hebrew is a feature of the bab, not a lacuna.

(The present rendering was made from the Arabic without consulting Nemoy 1930; principal points to check against him are the §3 Paul reductio phrasing and the §6 al-Maʾmūn analogy.)

- For Abū ʿĪsā al-Iṣfahānī and Yūdghān al-Rāʿī (§§1, 7): Q's own sect-catalogue in Anwar Maqala I (the ʿĪsāwiyya/Iṣfahāniyya and the Yūdghāniyya); Nemoy, HUCA 7 (1930) ad loc.; and for the wider context, the messianic-sectarian milieu treated by S. Pines, "The Jewish Christians of the Early Centuries," and by S. M. Wasserstrom, Between Muslim and Jew (1995), on Abū ʿĪsā.

- For the tawātur / tawāṭuʾ epistemology of transmitted report (§§2, 6): the Bahshamī treatment of al-khabar al-mutawātir as yielding ʿilm ḍarūrī — ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 15 (al-Tanabbuʾāt wa-l-Muʿjizāt) and vol. 16; and the standard uṣūl al-fiqh discussions (e.g., the impossibility of tawāṭuʾ across an uncollusive multitude). Q's distinction between transmitted khabar/mushāhada and inferred maʿqūl/qiyās (glossary §III) is squarely Bahshamī.

- For the muʿjiza as evidentiary sign of nubuwwa (§§1–3): ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 15 (al-Tanabbuʾāt wa-l-Muʿjizāt); Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa on al-nubuwwāt; glossary §VII anchor terms (nubuwwa, muʿjiza, iʿjāz). The criterion "a deed the like of which comes only from the Lord of the worlds, and only at the hand of a rasūl" (§2) is the standard kalām definition of the prophetic muʿjiza.

- For the anti-abrogation (taʾbīd al-sharīʿa / naskh) thread (§4): Bab 6 §§8–12 of this Maqala (the scriptural refutation of naskh); and on the Jewish anti-taḥrīf polemic that underlies the §6 al-Maʾmūn analogy, the parallel arguments in Saadia and later in the Karaite-Rabbanite anti-Islamic apologetic.

- For the early-vs-modern Muʿtazila on Jewish/Christian tawātur (§4): the positions of Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf (d. c. 227/841) and Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām (d. c. 231/845) — the qudamāʾ who credited it — against the muḥdathūn who restricted prophet-attestation to the Muslim transmission; see van Ess, Theologie und Gesellschaft, on al-Naẓẓām and Abū al-Hudhayl.

- For the "people were bound by their intellects" position refuted in Bab 14 (§6): Bab 14 of this Maqala (the refutation of the claim that, absent revelation, mankind was held to worship "by what was in their ʿuqūl" — which Q argues "issues in the nullification of prophethood"); and the back-reference to Bab 15 (the refutation of Muhammad's prophethood "from another angle," the al-maghāzī polemic that opens this file as the excluded Bab 15 tail).
